title: Australia and US aligned on AI rules: Charlton
full_text:
Washington | Andrew Charlton says measures such as protecting original work from large language models and making data centre developers supply their own energy are not at odds with Trump administration calls for a hands-off approach to regulating artificial intelligence.
Speaking to The Australian Financial Review by phone from the sidelines of a G20 innovation ministers meeting in North Carolina, the assistant technology minister said both governments were aligned on the need to seize the opportunities presented by the AI revolution.
"The key points that have come up today are the need, consistent with Australia's view ... that we need to be capturing the economic opportunity and making sure we put people at the centre and mitigate the risks, and we need to do those things simultaneously," Charlton said.
His comments came after Michael Kratsios, President Donald Trump's top technology adviser, opened the G20 meeting by urging member countries to avoid creating rules that could hamper the development of AI.
The Trump administration has advocated light-touch regulation to keep foreign governments out of the way of its national tech champions as they release ever-more powerful versions of AI models in the battle for supremacy over fast-moving Chinese rivals.
In what looked like a direct response to a growing national backlash against AI and its infrastructure, Trump himself weighed in this week, saying communities that turned away data centres would become "backwards and poor".
Kratsios, who is hosting the two-day summit with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, urged representatives from China, India and the European Union, as well as Australia, to avoid complex new rules to deal with AI.
"Slow policy adaptation makes it harder to capture the full benefits of innovation," he said.
"Policymakers do not need to approach each innovation in isolation and should not treat every emerging technology as a first-of-its-kind policy problem."
The summit is one of many ministerial meetings the US is hosting in the lead-up to the G20 leaders summit in Florida in December.
This week's gathering in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, included virtual appearances from industry titans such as SpaceX founder Elon Musk, Meta founder Mark Zuckerberg and OpenAI chief Sam Altman.
Charlton stopped in Silicon Valley on the way to the meeting this week to meet with leaders of companies such as Anthropic, Amazon, OpenAI and Google. He said he brought them up to speed on planned national AI standards that would govern their activities in Australia.
The outreach builds on Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's speech in July, in which he promised new laws by next year that will force developers to build new sources of energy generation to power data centres.
Albanese also committed to ensuring Australian artists and media companies can be compensated by AI labs that use their copyrighted material to train their large language models.
Charlton said he found a "pleasing level of support" for the proposals from the technology executives, and that neither policy push had dulled their appetite to invest. "Some of these companies are in pretty advanced planning for investment in Australia," he said.
Major AI companies are scouring the world to find new data centre locations, as the rapid and unfettered build-out in the US draws ever louder pushback over energy, water and noise concerns.
Charlton has been in talks with Anthropic about building data centres in Australia. However, he is not expected to land a deal out of his latest brief swing through Silicon Valley.
Anthropic told Australian data centre developers in July that it would buy any available capacity that could be delivered by the middle of next year as it aims to make Australia its second home for AI model training.
